title: SYSK Selects: Did a cow start the Great Chicago Fire?
summary: A Saturday Selects rerun of a July 2014-era episode asking whether Mrs. O'Leary's cow started the Great Chicago Fire of October 8-10, 1871. The hosts recount the fire's scale (about 3.5 square miles, roughly 17,450 buildings, about 300 deaths, nearly 100,000 homeless, roughly $192 million in damage), the wooden city and dry conditions, and the O'Leary family and barn at 137 DeKoven Street. They explain how the Chicago Tribune and reporter Michael Ahern spread the cow story, which Ahern later admitted making up. They then examine suspects: Mrs. O'Leary, who was asleep with a sore foot, the party guests who may have gone to the barn for milk, a comet theory, and neighbor Daniel "Peg Leg" Sullivan, whose testimony attorney Richard Bales later showed to be implausible. The episode closes with the fire's spread, firefighting failures, the O'Leary house being spared, the Chicago Fire Department training academy marking the barn site, and a listener mail story about a DEA raid triggered by a grow lamp.

segments.title: Selects intro
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Saturday Selects rerun of the Great Chicago Fire episode.

segments.title: Time-travel setup in 1871 Chicago
segments.summary: The hosts play a time-travel bit set in Chicago in October 1871, noting the wooden streets and sidewalks, dry weather, and dust.

segments.title: Scale of the Great Chicago Fire
segments.summary: The hosts give statistics on the fire: about 3.5 square miles destroyed, roughly 17,450 buildings, about 300 deaths, nearly 100,000 homeless, and about $192 million in damage. They note it was the third-deadliest or third-biggest US disaster of its kind.

segments.title: The O'Leary family and the barn
segments.summary: The O'Leary family lived at 137 DeKoven Street with a rented house and a barn holding cows, hay, coal, and wood shavings. The family was poor and working class, and Mrs. O'Leary sold milk in the neighborhood.

segments.title: Chicago Tribune and the cow myth
segments.summary: The Chicago Tribune initially blamed the O'Learys and a cow kicking over a lantern. Reporter Michael Ahern later confessed to making up the cow story, but it persisted in legend and song.

segments.title: Suspects: party guests, comet, and Mrs. O'Leary
segments.summary: Mrs. O'Leary testified that party guests went into the barn for milk and may have knocked over a lantern. A 2004 theory blamed a comet fragment, which the hosts dismiss as not possible. Mrs. O'Leary said she was asleep with a sore foot, and none of her property was insured.

segments.title: Daniel 'Peg Leg' Sullivan and the investigation
segments.summary: Neighbor Daniel Sullivan, who had a wooden leg, gave testimony placing him near the fire. Attorney Richard Bales mapped the area and showed his account was implausible. Lewis Cone later claimed he was gambling in the barn with an O'Leary son, which may have been boastful invention. The inquiry took about 1,100 pages of testimony.

segments.title: How the fire spread and was fought
segments.summary: The hosts describe firefighting failures: exhausted crews, damaged equipment, engines sent to the wrong address, a fire watcher who reported late, destroyed water pumps, and failed attempts to pump from Lake Michigan. Rain eventually ended the fire.

segments.title: Aftermath and legacy of the O'Leary family
segments.summary: The O'Leary house was spared. The site of the barn is marked by a cross at the Chicago Fire Department training academy. Mrs. O'Leary disliked publicity, chased away reporters, and turned down a job offer from P. T. Barnum's circus.

segments.title: Wrap-up of the Chicago fire episode
segments.summary: The hosts close the topic, noting Mrs. O'Leary was exonerated and remarking on the low death toll.

segments.title: Listener mail: DEA raid over grow lamp
segments.summary: A listener from New York describes an uncle whose saltwater aquarium lighting was mistaken for grow lights, leading to a DEA raid on the family home. The family reportedly received compensation.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts ask for family connections to the Chicago fire and sign off with a plug for the website search bar.
